lesson.menu_title: Hold On, I Have a Question
lesson.menu_desc: The interruption you did not see coming, and the four seconds before you answer -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- Hold On, I Have a Question
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Marcos Aurélio Miranda de Moura | Lesson 9 -- Hold On, I Have a Question
lesson.grammar_point: past continuous for background, with past simple for the interruption

listenings.text: I will tell you exactly when it happened, because I still think about it. I was presenting the second quarter and everything was going fine. I was explaining the coverage number, the room was following, and then somebody I did not know asked me whether the number included the two states we had just added. And I did not know. I hesitated, and the hesitation lasted about four seconds, and in my head those four seconds were an hour. What saved me was something a colleague told me years ago. Do not answer. Confirm the question first. So I said, let me make sure I have this right, you are asking whether the nineteen per cent includes the two new states. And while I was saying that, I remembered that it did not. Four seconds of talking bought me the answer. If I had tried to think in silence I would still be standing there.

The thing nobody tells you about answering a hard question in front of senior people is that silence feels four times longer to the person speaking than to the person listening. Four seconds of you thinking feels, to you, like the room has noticed and is judging you. To the room it is a normal pause, and honestly most of them were looking at their phones. So the fix is not to think faster. The fix is to buy the time out loud. Repeat the question. Ask whether you have understood it correctly. Say that you want to take a step back before you answer the detail. All of those are completely normal in a senior meeting and all of them give you three or four seconds, which is usually all you needed. And if you genuinely do not know, say so and give a date. Nobody has ever been fired for saying I will come back to you on Thursday. People have been fired for inventing a number.

We asked twenty senior executives what they actually notice when somebody is presenting in a second language, and the answers were remarkably consistent. Almost none of them mentioned grammar. Two mentioned accent, and both said it stopped mattering after a minute. What they noticed was whether the person could be interrupted and still find their way back. One of them put it very well. She said, I do not need you to be fluent. I need you to be findable. If I ask a question in the middle and you disappear for the rest of the meeting, that is the problem, and it is not a language problem. Several of them also said the same thing about pace. The people who sound most senior are not the fastest. They are the ones who pause before the important sentence, and everybody in the room leans in.
